_about: Plain-language guide for the Price paths & patterns view (paths-view.js): what each path model, analog method and family of price-action rules is, why it works, what it fits and what to watch, every abbreviation in full, and how the evidence is graded. Rule-by-rule texts come from app/price_action.py (rules.json).
intro: This page asks three questions about the next 13 weeks (63 trading days). How wide is the range of prices the stock could reach, when it moves together with the market, its sector and the stocks most like it? What happened after the moments in history that looked most like today? And what do the rule-based readings of the price bars say, and how much have those rules been worth out of sample?

None of it is a forecast of direction you should trade on. The ranges describe risk; the analogs and rules describe what followed similar situations in the past, and each method is scored against what actually happened after dates it had not seen. Where a method has not beaten simple benchmarks, the page says so.
paths_intro: Each model simulates hundreds of possible 63-day paths of the stock together with the S&P 500 ETF (SPY), its sector ETF and its two most correlated peers, from three years of daily returns. The fan shows the middle 50%, 80% and 90% of the simulated prices; the probabilities count the paths that end (or at some point fall) beyond a threshold; the joint figures read how often the stock fell 10% in the paths where the market or its sector fell 10% — the correlated part a single-stock model misses. The ensemble pools every model's paths.

ensemble.name: Ensemble (all seven models)
ensemble.what: Half of each model's paths pooled into one distribution.
ensemble.why: Every model has blind spots — thin tails, a fixed correlation, the assumption that the past repeats. Pooling them gives a range that no single model's error dominates.
ensemble.fits: The default view for every company.
ensemble.watch: If all the models share a blind spot — they all learn from the same three years — the ensemble shares it too.

joint_bootstrap.name: Joint bootstrap
joint_bootstrap.what: Each simulated day is a real day from the last three years, picked at random — the same day for every asset, so the stock, the market, the sector and the peers move as they actually moved together that day.
joint_bootstrap.why: It keeps the real correlation between assets and the real fat tails (big days happen as often as they did), with no formula imposed on either.
joint_bootstrap.fits: Every stock with three years of history; the plainest historical simulation.
joint_bootstrap.watch: Days are drawn independently, so calm and volatile spells get mixed: it misses volatility clustering and momentum. And it can only repeat days that already happened.

block_bootstrap.name: Block bootstrap (stationary bootstrap)
block_bootstrap.what: Like the joint bootstrap, but it copies whole runs of consecutive days (about two weeks on average, of random length — the stationary bootstrap of Politis and Romano, 1994) instead of single days.
block_bootstrap.why: Volatile days come in clusters and trends persist for a while; copying runs of days keeps both, so drawdowns are more realistic.
block_bootstrap.fits: Stocks whose volatility comes in waves — most of them.
block_bootstrap.watch: Still limited to what happened in the last three years; a run of days can only be as extreme as the worst one on file.

fhs.name: Filtered historical simulation (FHS)
fhs.what: First measures how volatile each day was relative to the conditions of the time with a GARCH model, which turns each historical return into a ‘shock’ in units of that day's volatility. Then it replays those shocks — the same day for every asset — scaled to today's volatility, letting volatility evolve along the path. Introduced by Barone-Adesi, Giannopoulos and Vosper (1999).
fhs.why: History repeats in shape, not in size: a 2% shock in a calm year is like a 4% shock in a turbulent one. Rescaling to today's volatility makes the range react when markets calm down or heat up.
fhs.fits: When today's volatility differs from the three-year average — after a crash or in an unusually quiet market.
fhs.watch: It trusts the GARCH model's reading of today's volatility; a sudden regime change can still surprise it.

factor.name: Factor model (market and sector)
factor.what: Each stock's daily return is split into the part explained by the market and its sector (its betas times their returns) and its own part. The market and sector are replayed from history together; each stock's own part is drawn separately.
factor.why: Most of what stocks have in common comes through a few common factors. Modelling correlation through them is the standard approach of risk models, and it keeps the stock's own risk apart from the market's.
factor.fits: Stocks whose co-movement is mostly the market and the sector; portfolios.
factor.watch: Peers that share something beyond the market and sector — a customer, a technology, a commodity — appear independent here, so joint losses can be understated.

cholesky.name: Correlated Brownian motion (Cholesky)
cholesky.what: Daily returns drawn from a multivariate normal distribution with the assets' average returns and their covariance matrix; the Cholesky decomposition of that matrix is the arithmetic that makes independent random numbers correlated. This is the textbook geometric Brownian motion behind the Black–Scholes model, for several assets at once.
cholesky.why: It is the classic, transparent benchmark: two numbers per asset and one correlation per pair describe everything.
cholesky.fits: A reference point; reasonable over long horizons where returns add up towards a normal shape.
cholesky.watch: Normal distributions have thin tails: crashes are far rarer in it than in real markets, and correlations stay fixed, while in a sell-off they rise. Expect it to understate losses.

t_copula.name: Student-t copula
t_copula.what: Separates two things: each asset's own distribution (taken from its history, fat tails included) and how the assets move together (the copula). The Student-t copula, with few degrees of freedom, makes extreme moves happen together more often than a normal copula would — stocks that are loosely related on calm days fall together in a crash.
t_copula.why: Tail dependence — everything falling at once — is what matters for losses and is exactly what correlation alone misses. The degrees of freedom are estimated from the data: the lower they are, the stronger the joint crashes.
t_copula.fits: Judging joint downside: the probability that the stock falls when the market falls.
t_copula.watch: Days are independent (no volatility clustering), and the dependence is symmetric: joint rallies are as strong as joint crashes.

dcc_garch.name: DCC-GARCH (dynamic conditional correlation)
dcc_garch.what: Each asset's volatility follows its own GARCH model, and the correlation between them changes over time too, rising and falling with recent joint moves (Engle, 2002). The simulation starts from today's volatilities and today's correlations and lets both evolve.
dcc_garch.why: Correlations are not constant: they jump in sell-offs, when diversification is needed most. Starting from today's correlation instead of a three-year average reflects the present.
dcc_garch.fits: Turbulent or changing markets; stocks whose link to the market has recently changed.
dcc_garch.watch: More parameters estimated, so more noise; normal shocks inside, so single-day tails are thinner than in the bootstrap models.

self.name: Own-history analogs
self.what: Takes the shape of the last 60 trading days of the stock's price (scaled by its own volatility) and searches the stock's whole history for the windows that looked most like it, then shows what the price did over the 63 days after each. The fan weighs closer matches more. This is the ‘method of analogues’ that Edward Lorenz proposed for weather (1969).
self.why: If markets repeat their behaviour in similar situations, the most similar past moments are the most informative guide to what comes next.
self.fits: Stocks with long histories; a check on the path models' symmetric view.
self.watch: A stock's own history holds few truly similar moments, and similar shapes can come from different causes. The ‘similarity’ score says how close the matches are; read the scorecard before trusting the direction.

pooled.name: Pooled analogs (every stock's history)
pooled.what: The same search across the histories of every stock on the site, not just this one, so there are thousands of candidate moments instead of dozens.
pooled.why: More candidates mean closer matches and a steadier estimate of what typically follows a given shape.
pooled.fits: Every company; the broadest analog view.
pooled.watch: Other stocks are not this stock: their analogs say what the shape usually led to, not what this company will do.

peers.name: Correlated assets
peers.what: The stocks and ETFs whose weekly returns have moved most closely with this stock over the last two years (Pearson correlation), and for each, whether its moves have tended to come first — the number of weeks by which it leads (lead–lag correlation, with a p-value corrected for testing several lags).
peers.why: Assets that share customers, suppliers, inputs or investors move together, and sometimes one reacts first. Knowing them shows where the stock's risk comes from and what to watch.
peers.watch: Correlation is not causation, and most apparent leads are noise; only leads with a small corrected p-value are used.

peer.name: Peer-conditional historical simulation
peer.what: Finds the past days when this stock and the basket of its most correlated assets (plus the market) had moved most like they have over the last week, month and quarter, and shows what this stock did over the next 63 days.
peer.why: It asks the question the user asked: when the assets that move with this stock last looked like this, how did the stock continue? It uses the group's situation, not just the stock's own chart.
peer.fits: Stocks with clear peers and long histories.
peer.watch: The peer group is today's; years ago the stock may have had different peers.

leadlag.name: Lead–lag forecast
leadlag.what: When some correlated assets have significantly led this stock, a regression (ordinary least squares, OLS) of the stock's next 21-day return on those leaders' recent returns, fitted on the last three years; the range comes from resampling the regression's errors.
leadlag.why: If news reaches one company's shares before another's, the first one's move carries information about the second's.
leadlag.fits: Only stocks with a statistically significant leader.
leadlag.watch: Leads are rare and fragile: markets arbitrage them away. Shown only when one passes the significance test.

naive.name: Naive baseline
naive.what: The stock's own distribution of 63-day returns over the last year, used as the forecast every time.
naive.why: Any method worth reading should beat this simple benchmark out of sample.

candlestick.name: Candlestick patterns
candlestick.what: Shapes of one to three daily bars — the body between open and close, the wicks to the high and low — read since 18th-century Japanese rice trading and brought to Western markets by Steve Nison (1991). A long lower wick after a fall (hammer) says sellers pushed the price down and buyers pushed it back.

brooks.name: Al Brooks price action
brooks.what: Reading the market bar by bar, as taught by Al Brooks: first whether it is trending or in a trading range, then which side is ‘always in’ (would hold a position now), then pullbacks counted by legs (a second-leg pullback in a trend, H2 / L2, is a classic entry), wedges (three pushes) and whether breakouts follow through or fail.

structure.name: Market structure (Dow theory)
structure.what: An uptrend is a series of higher highs and higher lows (HH, HL); a downtrend, lower highs and lower lows (LH, LL). A close beyond the last swing in the trend's direction is a break of structure (BOS); a close beyond the opposite swing is a change of character (CHoCH), the first sign of a reversal. The idea goes back to Charles Dow's editorials around 1900.

pattern.name: Classic chart patterns
pattern.what: Head and shoulders, double tops and bottoms, triangles, flags and cup-and-handle, found by algorithm on a smoothed price, as Lo, Mamaysky and Wang (2000) did to test whether they carry information. The signal is the breakout that completes the pattern.

wyckoff.name: Wyckoff method
wyckoff.what: Richard Wyckoff's reading (1930s) of how large investors accumulate before a rise and distribute before a fall: a trading range after a trend, a ‘spring’ (a dip below the range that is quickly bought back) or an ‘upthrust’ (a pop above it that fails), then a breakout — markup or markdown.

vsa.name: Volume spread analysis (VSA)
vsa.what: Tom Williams' development of Wyckoff: each bar is read from its spread (high minus low), its volume and where it closes. A wide down bar on huge volume that closes off its low can be ‘stopping volume’; an up bar on low volume, ‘no demand’.

profile.name: Volume profile / market profile
profile.what: How much volume traded at each price over a period, from Peter Steidlmayer's market profile at the Chicago Board of Trade. The price with the most volume is the point of control (POC); the band holding 70% of the volume is the value area (VAH to VAL, value area high and low); high- and low-volume nodes (HVN, LVN) tend to act as magnets and gaps.

levels.name: Support, resistance and supply / demand zones
levels.what: Prices where the stock has turned several times (support below, resistance above), and the zones a strong move started from (demand below, supply above), where orders may remain.

ict.name: ICT / smart money concepts (SMC)
ict.what: A popular modern school, from Michael Huddleston (‘The Inner Circle Trader’): fair value gaps (FVG, a three-bar gap a fast move leaves), order blocks (the last opposite bar before such a move), liquidity sweeps (a wick beyond an obvious high or low that reverses) and premium / discount (above or below the middle of the range). Rule-based versions here; the school itself has little published evidence.

elliott.name: Elliott wave
elliott.what: R. N. Elliott's idea (1938) that trends move in five waves and corrections in three (A-B-C). Implemented here only with the three hard rules — wave 2 never goes past the start of wave 1, wave 3 is never the shortest, wave 4 does not overlap wave 1 — on swings measured in multiples of the average true range (ATR). Wave counts are notoriously subjective.

quant.name: Quantitative price rules with academic evidence
quant.what: Breakouts of the 20- and 55-day range (Donchian channels, used by the Turtle traders), time-series momentum (Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen, 2012: the last year's return, excluding the latest month, tends to persist), nearness to the 52-week high (George and Hwang, 2004) and short-term reversal (Jegadeesh, 1990: last month's extreme moves tend to partly reverse).

evidence.how: Every rule is run on every stock's daily bars since about 2016 with no look-ahead (a swing point counts only once it is confirmed). For each signal the return over the next 5, 20 and 60 trading days is compared with the same stock's average return over that horizon, signed by the rule's direction, so a positive number means the rule worked. Signals before 2021 are the in-sample period; 2021 onwards is out of sample. Standard errors are clustered by month, since many stocks signal at once. Testing many rules makes some look good by chance, so the out-of-sample p-values are corrected with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure (false discovery rate 10%).

grades.strong: Significant out of sample after the multiple-testing correction, with the same sign in sample.
grades.moderate: p below 5% out of sample, but not after the correction.
grades.weak: Only significant in the earlier, in-sample years.
grades.none: No reliable difference from the stock's average.

scorecard: The scorecard runs each method at past dates on a fixed sample of companies, using only data available before each date, and compares its 63-day range with what happened. A well-calibrated 80% range contains the outcome about 80% of the time; the pinball loss scores the whole distribution (lower is better); skill is the improvement over the naive baseline (positive is better).
glossary: A model in which today's volatility depends on yesterday's volatility and yesterday's shock, so calm and turbulent spells persist (Bollerslev, 1986).
Historical returns rescaled by a GARCH model to today's volatility, then replayed.
Correlations between assets that change over time with their recent joint moves (Engle, 2002).
The part of a joint distribution that describes how variables move together, separated from each one's own distribution.
Degrees of freedom of the Student-t
Lower values mean fatter tails and, in a t copula, more joint extremes.
Simulating by drawing at random, with replacement, from what actually happened.
Running the same random experiment many times and studying the spread of results.
The largest fall from a peak to a later trough along a path.
An exchange-traded fund tracking the S&P 500; used as ‘the market’.
A fund that trades on an exchange like a single stock.
The standard way to fit a straight-line relationship.
The average daily range of a stock, counting gaps between days (J. Welles Wilder, 1978).
An average of past prices that weighs recent days more.
Higher high, higher low, lower high, lower low
The swing points that define up- and downtrends.
A close beyond the last swing point in the trend's direction.
A close beyond the last swing point against the trend: a possible reversal.
The second attempt to resume a trend after a pullback: a bar whose high (low) exceeds the prior bar's for the second time.
A gap between bar 1's high and bar 3's low (or the reverse) left by a fast move.
The last opposite-coloured bar before a move that breaks structure.
The ICT school's vocabulary for institutional order flow.
The online name of Michael Huddleston, whose concepts are implemented as rules here.
The price with the most traded volume in a period.
Value area high, value area low
The edges of the price band that held 70% of the volume.
Prices with unusually much or little traded volume.
Reading each bar by its range, volume and close.
Data the method did not see when it was set up — here 2021 onwards.
A correction for testing many rules at once that keeps the share of false discoveries near a chosen level (10% here).
How likely a result at least this strong would be if the rule had no effect; small is better.
A score for a forecast range: it penalizes outcomes outside each quantile, weighted by how far.
Where the actual outcome fell within the forecast distribution; for a well-calibrated forecast it is spread evenly from 0 to 1.
The correlation of one asset's return with another's return some weeks later.
